strengths: Provides a genuine theoretical contribution establishing exact equivalence between local-SSL weight updates and global BP-SSL gradients in deep linear networks under precise, clearly stated conditions (Theorem 3.1), with rigorous proofs (including batched version in the appendix).

The theory is not merely descriptive but generative: it motivates concrete algorithmic modifications (direct feedback from the top layer, Theorem 3.3; 2D spatially dependent projection matrices for convnets) that are then validated both by gradient-alignment simulations and downstream task performance, creating a coherent theory-to-practice pipeline.

Strong empirical results: the proposed CLAPP++ variants set a new state of the art among local-SSL methods on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny-ImageNet, and the best variant closes much of the historical performance gap with backpropagation-based SSL, which the authors note has not been previously achieved in the SSL setting.

Careful ablation studies (Table 2, Figure 5) isolate the contribution of each theory-driven modification (data augmentation choice, spatial dependence, direct feedback), showing consistent, interpretable trends rather than an opaque bag of tricks.

Valuable negative-result appendix showing that other bio-plausible BP-approximation frameworks (DFA, predictive coding) fail to optimize self-supervised objectives, which contextualizes why the paper focuses on local-SSL-specific constructions rather than generic BP-approximators.

Good connection to biological plausibility (Hebbian interpretation, apical dendrite gating, structured cortical feedback), tying the mathematical results back to the neuroscience motivation stated in the introduction.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility details in the appendix (architectures, hyperparameters, augmentation pipelines, training details) for the main experiments.
weaknesses: The central exact-equivalence theorem relies on strong, unrealistic assumptions (deep linear network, orthonormal square weight matrices, unconstrained trainable B^l), which are explicitly acknowledged to break down for nonlinear/CNN architectures; extensions to more realistic settings (Theorem 3.3, spatial dependence) are proven only for restricted cases (e.g., f linear, batch size one) and otherwise rely on numerical simulation rather than proof, weakening the theoretical guarantees underlying the practical algorithmic recommendations.

The claim that local-SSL 'matches' global BP-SSL rests on a BP-InfoNCE/BP-CLAPP++ baseline that the authors themselves note is not state-of-the-art global SSL (linear projection head, VGG backbone rather than nonlinear heads/ResNet), so the comparison, while informative, is against a relatively weak proxy for true global BP-SSL performance rather than the strongest attainable baseline.

Some of the theory-motivated increments (direct feedback, CLAPP++DFB vs CLAPP++) yield small improvements that are close to or within the reported confidence intervals on some datasets (e.g., STL-10), raising questions about the practical significance of that particular component in isolation, even though the combined CLAPP++both model shows more clearly significant gains.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small-scale datasets (CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny-ImageNet) with a single VGG-style architecture; there is no evidence of how the approach scales to larger datasets (e.g., ImageNet) or more modern architectures (ResNets, transformers), leaving open questions about generality.

The paper is notation-heavy with many overlapping symbols (B^l, c^l, multiple loss types, f functions across algorithms) that, despite the unifying Table 1, may still be difficult for readers to parse quickly, particularly in the theoretical sections.
No explicit statement of code/data release for reproducibility, despite fairly detailed methodological descriptions in the appendix.
The Impact Statement is generic boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential implications of the work (e.g., for neuromorphic hardware deployment or broader ML use).

strengths: Provides a genuinely novel theoretical link between local-SSL algorithms (CLAPP, Forward-Forward-like rules) and global BP-SSL in deep linear networks, with rigorous proofs (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2, Theorem 3.3) showing exact or improved gradient equivalence under specified conditions.

The theory is not just descriptive but generative: it directly motivates two concrete algorithmic modifications (2D spatially-dependent feedback projections and direct top-down feedback), and both are shown empirically to increase gradient cosine-similarity with BP-SSL as predicted.

Strong, carefully controlled empirical validation across three datasets (CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny-ImageNet), with multiple random seeds and confidence intervals, plus ablations isolating the contribution of each proposed component (Table 2, Figure 5).

The resulting CLAPP++ variants set a new state of the art among local-SSL methods and close much of the gap to a comparable global BP-SSL baseline, which is a first for SSL in this local-learning literature.

Useful negative results/controls: the paper shows that other bio-plausible BP-approximation frameworks (DFA, Predictive Coding) fail to optimize SSL objectives, contextualizing why the CLAPP-based approach is preferable and strengthening the paper's overall narrative.
Clear, well-organized presentation with a unifying notation (Table 1) that cleanly encompasses several existing local-SSL algorithms (CLAPP, Forward-Forward, PhyLL, SCFF), aiding conceptual clarity.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information in the appendix (architectures, hyperparameters, training procedures, proofs).
weaknesses: The core theorems require idealized conditions (orthonormal/semi-orthonormal weight matrices, linear networks, instantaneous B-optimum) that are quite far from the practical nonlinear convnet setting; the extension to CNNs (spatial dependence) is justified mostly by intuition and simulation rather than a formal theorem, so the link between theory and the final practical algorithm is partly heuristic.

The BP-SSL baseline (BP-InfoNCE / BP-CLAPP++) used for the 'matches BP-SSL' claim uses a simple linear projection head and the same VGG backbone rather than a well-tuned, strong global SSL baseline (e.g., SimCLR/ResNet); the authors themselves note it is not state-of-the-art BP-SSL, which weakens the strength of the headline claim that local-SSL 'matches' backpropagation.

Absolute performance gains of the theoretically motivated DFB variant over CLAPP++ are fairly small (e.g., STL-10: 78.66 -> 79.38-79.62), so while statistically consistent, the practical significance of the direct-feedback contribution specifically (as opposed to spatial dependence, which is the dominant factor) is more modest.

Evaluation is restricted to relatively small-scale, low-resolution image datasets and a single fixed VGG-style architecture; scalability of the proposed spatial-dependence scheme (with its increased parameter/memory cost for many B^l matrices) to deeper or higher-resolution settings is not analyzed.

Table 2 comparisons mix numbers taken directly from prior papers with the authors' own reproductions under a different augmentation/training pipeline, which slightly complicates apples-to-apples comparison across methods despite the authors' effort to standardize this.

strengths: Provides a genuinely novel theoretical contribution: a common formalism unifying CLAPP, Forward-Forward, PhyLL, and SCFF, followed by rigorous proofs (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2, Theorem 3.3, Proposition 3.5) establishing precise conditions under which local-SSL updates exactly match global BP-SSL updates in deep linear (and semi-orthonormal/convolutional linear) networks.

The theory-to-practice pipeline is unusually tight: each theoretical insight (orthonormality breaking with shrinking width motivating direct feedback; lack of spatial dependence in BP gradients motivating 2D spatial B^l) is first validated numerically in simplified linear/ReLU-MLP settings (Figures 2-4) and then translated into concrete algorithmic modifications (CLAPP++, DFB, spatial dependence) that are tested at scale.

Strong, comprehensive empirical validation across four datasets (CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet) with multiple seeds and confidence intervals, careful ablations (Table 2, Figure 5) isolating the contribution of each theory-motivated component, and consistent correlation between gradient-alignment improvements and downstream accuracy improvements.

New state-of-the-art results among local-SSL methods on all four benchmarks, and closing (or nearly closing) the gap to comparable BP-SSL baselines (BP-CLAPP++, BP-InfoNCE) on three of the four datasets, which is a notable achievement given the historically large performance gap between local and global SSL.

Includes a valuable negative control: naive application of other biologically plausible BP-approximation frameworks (DFA, Predictive Coding) to the same SSL objective fails to achieve competitive performance (Appendix D), which helps justify why the specific CLAPP-based construction is needed rather than existing generic BP-approximation machinery.

Practical significance is quantified via VRAM and wall-clock benchmarking (Table 3), showing meaningful memory savings (38-60%) for local-SSL relative to BP-SSL, relevant for neuromorphic/energy-efficient hardware applications mentioned in the introduction.

Reasonably honest discussion of limitations (architecture scale limited to VGG-style CNNs, gap remains on ImageNet, open challenge of extending to residual connections) and a plausible, appropriately hedged discussion connecting the CLAPP++DFB mechanism to apical dendrite biology.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are restricted to deep linear (or semi-linear with linear f) networks with strong assumptions (orthonormal/semi-orthonormal weights, batch size one in the core proofs, convexity of f, instantaneous B^l optimization); the leap to nonlinear ReLU MLPs and convnets is validated only empirically via cosine similarity trends, not proven, so the central practical claims rest on an extrapolation whose scope of validity is not fully characterized.

The performance gap between local-SSL and BP-SSL is not closed on ImageNet, the most realistic/large-scale dataset tested (CLAPP++DFB: 44.16 vs BP-CLAPP++: 48.52, vs BP-InfoNCE: 55.19), which somewhat undercuts the headline claim that local-SSL matches global BP-SSL, particularly as complexity/resolution scales up.

All experiments use a fixed VGG-style convolutional architecture; there is no evaluation on residual networks, transformers, or other modern architectures that dominate practical self-supervised learning, and the authors explicitly note that extending to residual connections is nontrivial and left to future work, limiting the demonstrated generality of the approach.

The BP-InfoNCE baseline is explicitly acknowledged as not representing SOTA global BP-SSL (linear projection head, VGG backbone rather than nonlinear heads/ResNets), so the 'matches BP-SSL' claims are made against a deliberately weakened/matched baseline rather than against strong standard SSL pipelines, which somewhat limits the significance of the comparison for practitioners interested in state-of-the-art SSL performance.

The 2D spatial-dependence modification substantially increases the parameter count of B^l (scaling with image/patch size), and while VRAM savings are still reported, the added parameter overhead and its implications for the 'locality'/efficiency motivation of local learning are not fully discussed or ablated against a matched parameter budget.

Confidence intervals are computed from only 4 random seeds, which is a fairly small number for establishing statistical robustness of the reported accuracy differences, several of which are numerically small (e.g., CLAPP++ vs CLAPP++DFB on CIFAR-10).

The paper's own code repository link appears blank in the provided manuscript, raising a reproducibility concern (though this may be an artifact of anonymization/formatting rather than an actual omission).

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely novel theoretical unification of several disparate local-SSL algorithms (CLAPP, Forward-Forward, PhyLL, SCFF) under a common notation (Table 1), which is a useful conceptual contribution to the community.

Theorem 3.1 and its extensions (Corollary 3.2, Theorem 3.3, Proposition 3.5) rigorously identify precise conditions under which local-SSL updates are exactly equal to (or provably closer to) global BP-SSL updates in deep linear networks; the proofs appear careful and are given in full in the appendix.

The theory-to-practice pipeline is well executed: insights from the linear-network analysis (direct feedback, spatial dependence) are translated into concrete algorithmic modifications (CLAPP++, CLAPP++DFB) that are then empirically validated first via gradient cosine similarity and then via downstream classification accuracy, closing an unusually tight loop between theory and empirical outcome.

Broad empirical validation across four datasets (CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet) with several ablations, multiple seeds with confidence intervals, and comparisons against a wide range of baselines (SCFF, SoftHebb, LPL, Stochastic FF, naive DFA/Predictive-Coding baselines) sets a new state of the art for local-SSL on the tested benchmarks.

The paper is transparent about negative results (Appendix D: DFA and predictive-coding baselines fail to optimize SSL objectives) and reports practical costs/benefits (VRAM and wall-clock comparisons in Table 3), which strengthens the credibility and reproducibility of the empirical claims.

The biological plausibility discussion connecting CLAPP++DFB and 2D spatial dependence to known cortical circuit motifs (apical dendrite feedback, structured visual cortex connectivity) adds interpretive value, though it is appropriately framed as speculative.
weaknesses: The central theoretical results (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2, Proposition 3.5) rely on strong idealized assumptions (deep linear networks, orthonormal or semi-orthonormal weight matrices, patch size 1, no nonlinearity/max-pooling, batch-independent or instantaneous B optimum) that do not hold in the practical convolutional non-linear networks used in the experiments; the extension to realistic settings is empirical/heuristic ("theory indicates... numerically we show"), which somewhat undercuts the claimed theoretical grounding of the proposed algorithmic changes.

The headline claim that local-SSL "matches" global BP-SSL is weakest exactly on the hardest, most realistic benchmark (ImageNet), where CLAPP++DFB (44.16%) remains well below both BP-CLAPP++ (48.52%) and especially BP-InfoNCE (55.19%); the paper's positive framing in the abstract somewhat overstates this gap.

The BP-SSL comparison baselines (BP-CLAPP++, BP-InfoNCE) are explicitly acknowledged as not state-of-the-art (linear projection heads, VGG rather than ResNet architecture), so "matching BP-SSL" is a comparison against a deliberately weakened target rather than a strong, competitive global SSL baseline, limiting the significance of the performance claims.

The 2D spatial-dependence trick, while theoretically motivated, substantially increases the size/parameter count of the learnable projection matrix B^l (growing with image resolution); the paper does not clearly quantify or discuss this parameter/memory trade-off, which is relevant given that reduced memory footprint is touted as a practical benefit of local learning (Table 3 only accounts for activation memory, not the growing B^l parameters).

Even with all proposed improvements, the cosine similarity between local-SSL and BP-SSL gradients remains fairly low in early layers (Figures 2-4), and the paper does not fully explain the disconnect between still-limited gradient alignment and the near-parity classification performance, leaving the mechanistic story incomplete.

No experiments on more modern/scalable architectures (ResNets, skip connections) or truly large-scale datasets are provided; the paper acknowledges this as future work, but it limits confidence that the approach and its theoretical insights will generalize beyond the specific VGG-style CNNs studied.

Confidence intervals are computed from only 4 random seeds, which is a fairly small sample for the accuracy differences being emphasized (e.g., CLAPP++ vs CLAPP++DFB vs CLAPP++both), making some comparative claims between closely performing variants less statistically robust.

strengths: Develops a genuinely novel and rigorous theoretical framework (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2, Theorem 3.3, Proposition 3.5) that formally connects local self-supervised learning rules (CLAPP, Forward-Forward, PhyLL, SCFF) to global BP-SSL gradients under precise, clearly stated conditions (orthonormal weights, learnable unconstrained B, no normalization), including full proofs in the appendix for both batch-size-one and batched settings.

The theory is not merely descriptive but directly generative: it motivates two concrete, non-trivial algorithmic modifications (2D spatially-dependent feedback matrices and direct top-down feedback) that are shown analytically and numerically to increase gradient alignment with BP-SSL, and these same modifications translate into measurable downstream performance gains, establishing a credible causal link between theory and practice.

Strong, broad empirical validation across four datasets (CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet) with multiple ablations (Table 2, Figure 5) isolating the contribution of each theoretical insight; the resulting CLAPP++ variants set a new state of the art among local-SSL methods and close (or nearly close) the gap with comparable BP-SSL baselines on three of four datasets.

The paper thoughtfully evaluates alternative existing bio-plausible BP-approximation frameworks (Direct Feedback Alignment, Predictive Coding) on the same SSL objectives and shows they fail to reach competitive performance, which contextualizes why the paper focuses on local-SSL rules and strengthens the significance of the contribution.
Practical/systems-level analysis of VRAM and wall-clock savings (Table 3) adds a useful applied angle beyond the purely representational-quality question.

Very thorough appendix (explicit training details, algorithms, hyperparameter tables, additional ablations on rank-constrained B and gradient alignment across training stages) supports reproducibility.

The discussion connects the mathematical constructs (direct feedback, spatial dependence) back to concrete, falsifiable biological hypotheses about apical dendrite function and cortical connectivity, adding conceptual value for computational neuroscience audiences without overclaiming.
weaknesses: The core theorems require restrictive idealized conditions (deep linear networks, orthonormal or semi-orthonormal weight matrices, B allowed to reach its unconstrained optimum instantaneously) that do not hold in the nonlinear convolutional networks used in the actual experiments; the leap from linear theory to nonlinear practice is bridged only empirically (gradient cosine-similarity plots), so the theoretical guarantees do not strictly explain the empirical gains, only motivate them.

On the largest and most realistic benchmark (ImageNet), local-SSL still falls meaningfully short of the BP-SSL baseline (e.g., CLAPP++DFB 44.16 vs BP-CLAPP++ 48.52, and further behind BP-InfoNCE at 55.19), somewhat undercutting the strong framing in the abstract/title that local learning "matches" BP-SSL.

Experiments are confined to VGG-style architectures without residual connections or batch/layer normalization schemes common in modern SSL pipelines; the paper acknowledges this but does not provide any preliminary evidence or analysis of how the theory would extend to skip connections, which are central to virtually all contemporary large-scale vision backbones.

The BP-SSL and BP-InfoNCE baselines used for comparison are deliberately kept architecture-matched (linear projection head, same VGG) and are explicitly noted as not being SOTA for global SSL, which makes the "local-SSL matches BP-SSL" claim somewhat narrower than it may appear at first reading — it is a claim about matching a specific, non-optimized global baseline rather than closing the gap with best-in-class global SSL.

The 2D spatial-dependence mechanism grows the feedback matrix size linearly with image resolution/feature map size, which raises scalability concerns for higher-resolution inputs or deeper/wider networks beyond the tested regimes; this trade-off is not extensively quantified beyond the reported VRAM table for the specific architectures tested.

Statistical robustness is based on only 4 random seeds for confidence intervals, and several rows in the comparison table (Table 2) are missing entries for prior methods, making some cross-method comparisons incomplete or reliant on differing architectures/protocols from the original papers.
